description: A composite figure in two blocks. (a) and (b) are simulation field maps of the dislocation-density increment ρ−ρ0, drawn as 3 × 1 arrays sharing one colour bar labelled "ρ−ρ0 (×10^14 m^-2)" running from 2 (dark blue) to 23 (dark red). Column headers read ε=0.0 %, ε=5.0 % and ε=11.0 %, under an arrow annotated "Increment of dislocation density with global strain". Row (a) is labelled "Fe–TiB2 steel" (homogeneous α-ferrite matrix); row (b) is labelled "Our LDS" (heterogeneous triplex steel). At ε=0.0 % both rows are nearly uniform dark blue, i.e. close to the initial dislocation density. With straining, (a) develops narrow high-intensity yellow/red bands oriented roughly 45° to the horizontal, leaving dark, almost undeformed islands that are boxed by red circles at ε=11.0 %; (b) instead spreads moderate cyan/green increments through the austenite, and its red circles plus orange dashed outlines mark shear bands that reappear only at ε=11 %. Panel (c) plots True stress (MPa, 0–1000) versus True strain (0.00–0.12): the experimental "Our LDS" curve (open grey circles) rises steeply and approaches just below the 800 MPa gridline at ε ≈ 0.11, while stacked simulated colour fields assign the flow stress to Austenite (blue, largest), δ-ferrite (red, nearly constant band) and TiB2 (orange, smallest, elastic load-bearing). The caption states δ-ferrite contributes ~170 MPa, >30 % of overall yield strength. The group argues that the heterogeneous matrix homogenises plasticity and distributes dislocation hardening, giving higher strength without shear-band-driven failure.

subfigures.description: Three simulated maps of dislocation-density increment ρ−ρ0 for the conventional "Fe–TiB2 steel" at ε=0.0 %, 5.0 % and 11.0 %, on the shared colour bar (2–23 ×10^14 m^-2). At ε=0.0 % the map is uniformly dark blue; at 5.0 % and 11.0 % narrow yellow/red shear bands at roughly 45° to the loading axis appear, and red circles at ε=11.0 % mark dark, nearly undeformed zones.

The same three strain states for "Our LDS" on the same colour scale. Increments spread as diffuse cyan/green fields through the austenite rather than concentrating into narrow bands; red circles and orange dashed outlines at ε=11.0 % mark reappearing shear bands (orange, per the caption/citation).

True stress (MPa, 0–1000) versus true strain (0.00–0.12) with legend "Exp:" Our LDS (open grey circles joined by a line) and "Sim:" Austenite (blue), δ-ferrite (red), TiB2 (orange) stacked areas. The experimental curve is still rising at the last plotted strain and lies just below the 800 MPa gridline.

observations.observation: Panels (a) and (b) share a single colour bar labelled "ρ−ρ0 (×10^14 m^-2)" with only its two end values printed, 23 (top, dark red) and 2 (bottom, dark blue).
The column headers of the map arrays are ε=0.0 %, ε=5.0 % and ε=11.0 %, with an arrow above reading "Increment of dislocation density with global strain".
Row (a) is labelled "Fe–TiB2 steel" and row (b) is labelled "Our LDS"; both rows show the same three global strain levels.
At ε=0.0 % both map rows are almost entirely dark blue, corresponding to values near the low end of the ρ−ρ0 scale.

In row (a) (Fe–TiB2 steel) the high-intensity yellow/red regions form narrow elongated bands inclined at approximately 45° to the horizontal at ε=5.0 % and ε=11.0 %, while the remainder of the map stays blue.
Red circles drawn on row (a) at ε=11.0 % enclose regions that remain dark blue, i.e. with negligible dislocation-density increment, enclosed by high-increment surroundings.
Row (b) (Our LDS) at ε=5.0 % and ε=11.0 % shows widespread cyan/green increments across most of the field, in contrast to the banded pattern of row (a) at the same strains.
Red circles and orange dashed outlines are drawn on row (b) at ε=11.0 %, marking orange-coloured shear bands that reappear only at that late strain stage.
Panel (c) axes are labelled "True stress (MPa)" (0 to 1000) and "True strain" (0.00 to 0.12).
Panel (c) legend lists "Exp:" Our LDS (open grey circles with a connecting line) and "Sim:" with colour fields Austenite (blue), δ-ferrite (red) and TiB2 (orange).

In panel (c) the experimental "Our LDS" curve rises steeply at low strain and, at the final plotted strain near 0.11, lies slightly below the 800 MPa gridline; the simulated stacked areas sum to give the overall flow stress.

In panel (c) the simulated austenite field (blue) occupies the largest share of the stacked area and widens with strain, the δ-ferrite field (red) forms a band of nearly constant thickness, and the TiB2 field (orange) is the thinnest.

The caption states that the strengthening contribution of δ-ferrite remains almost constant at 170 MPa and accounts for >30 % of the overall yield strength, while the austenite contribution increases with straining.

The caption states that the TiB2 strengthening contribution is treated as an elastic load-bearing phase because the particles are micron-sized and boundary-localized and cannot act as Orowan obstacles.

The citing text states that in the heterogeneous matrix of the present steel the dislocation density is more uniformly distributed at values on the order of 10^15 m^-2, whereas in conventional Fe–TiB2 steel the undeformed zones retain low densities close to the initial values.

The citing text states that shear bands in the conventional Fe–TiB2 steel form at approximately 45° to the loading axis and persist throughout deformation, and that red circles in Fig. 12(a) indicate zones of minimal deformation caused by stress shielding from rigid particles.
